reason: Anyone can send malformed heartbeat requests and read up to 64 KB of server memory per request, and this was exploited at mass scale. I chose partial over total because each read returns random memory chunks; private keys and passwords can leak, but not all data on demand.
salesperson_line: Anyone online can repeatedly pull chunks of this server's memory, which can contain passwords, session cookies or its encryption key.

reason: The host shows signs it has already been taken over, typically by automated campaigns hitting databases with no login. The attacker already holds full control of the data.
salesperson_line: An attacker appears to already be inside this system and can read, change or delete everything on it.

reason: Automated ransom campaigns find databases with no login, copy or wipe their contents, and leave a payment demand. The data has already been changed or destroyed.
salesperson_line: Someone has already wiped or locked this data and left a ransom demand; the original data may be gone or stolen.

reason: Anyone can connect without credentials and read, change or drop every database. Wipe-and-ransom campaigns against these servers are well documented, and the first evidence sample already contains a ransom database.
salesperson_line: Anyone on the internet can read, copy, change or delete everything in this database without a password.

reason: Without a password, anyone can read and write every key. Redis's own config commands are widely abused to write files and plant crypto-mining malware.
salesperson_line: Anyone can read or erase all stored data, and attackers commonly use this opening to take over the whole server.

reason: An unauthenticated Elasticsearch server lets anyone query, download and delete every index. Automated wipe-and-ransom campaigns target exactly these servers.
salesperson_line: Anyone can search, download or delete all the data in this search database without logging in.

reason: With no login, anyone can list and usually download images, which often contain source code and built-in secrets. I chose poc over active because I don't know of widespread abuse campaigns, and partial over total because a listing doesn't prove downloads or uploads are allowed.
salesperson_line: Anyone can see and likely download this company's software packages, which often contain passwords and internal code.

reason: Bots mass-scan for anonymous FTP to grab files or store illicit content on writable folders. Access is limited to what the anonymous account can see, so partial.
salesperson_line: Anyone can log in to this file server without a password and browse, download, or possibly upload files.

reason: Anyone can list share names with a null session using standard tools. I chose information over partial because listing shares doesn't prove their files can be read, and poc over active because the abuse is not confirmed for share listing on its own.
salesperson_line: Anyone can see the names of this company's shared network folders, a first step toward getting at the files inside.

reason: Anyone can connect to the remote desktop with no password and control the keyboard and screen. Exposed VNC with no login is mass-scanned and abused.
salesperson_line: Anyone on the internet can take over this computer's screen and keyboard, with no password needed.

reason: The device sends its admin password in plain text to a simple query, and the attacker then logs in and reconfigures it and the equipment connected through it. A public method has existed for years; I know of no credible reports of widespread abuse.
salesperson_line: This device gives its admin password to anyone who asks, letting them control it and the equipment connected to it.

reason: Anyone can open the admin page and change settings, send jobs, or redirect scans. Torn between total and partial for printer-level control, I chose partial; torn between poc and active, I chose poc.
salesperson_line: Anyone can open this printer's admin settings, change them, print to it, or possibly see scanned documents.

reason: Exposed Ollama, ComfyUI and similar servers are mass-scanned and abused to run free AI workloads, pull or delete models, and in ComfyUI's case to install malicious add-ons. I chose partial because the products differ and full system control is not shown for all of them.
salesperson_line: Anyone can use this company's AI server for free, run up its costs, and tamper with or delete its models.

reason: Many of these protocols have no login, so anyone can read and write control values. Internet-exposed controllers have been tampered with by state-linked groups. Some listed protocols support authentication, so I chose partial over total.
salesperson_line: Anyone online can talk directly to this industrial equipment's controls and may be able to read or change how it runs.

reason: With the published key, an attacker on the network path can pose as the server and capture logins. That requires a position between user and server, and I rated it partial because it captures sessions, not the system itself.
salesperson_line: Someone positioned between staff and this device could pose as it and steal the passwords people type in.

reason: The finding is a generic, unconfirmed version-based guess, so its severity depends on which CVE is listed and whether it is really present. The example CVEs are rated separately below.
salesperson_line: This system's version may have known security holes, but they haven't been confirmed yet.

reason: These fuel-tank gauges accept commands with no login, so anyone can read inventory and change tank names, alarm limits and settings. Exposed gauges are mass-scanned and have been tampered with. It is partial because it controls gauge settings, not the fuel system as a whole.
salesperson_line: Anyone can see this station's fuel levels and could change gauge settings or alarms, disrupting how the station operates.

reason: Anyone can list folder names using a plain rsync client. I chose information over partial because a listing doesn't prove the folders can be downloaded without credentials.
salesperson_line: Anyone can see the names of this company's synced folders, which reveal staff names and hint at what data is stored.

reason: IPMI 2.0 hands any requester a password hash to crack offline, and Metasploit automates that step. Logging in still requires cracking that server's own password, so automatable is no. I chose poc because I'm not sure abuse is widespread. A successful login gives full control of the server's hardware.
salesperson_line: An attacker could grab a scrambled admin password, crack it, and take full control of this server from outside.

reason: Internet-facing ESXi was hit by mass ransomware such as ESXiArgs. Being reachable alone still requires either valid credentials or an unpatched flaw that this finding doesn't confirm. Compromising the host gives total control of every virtual machine on it.
salesperson_line: The system running all this company's servers is reachable online; ransomware gangs actively target these to lock everything at once.

reason: Attackers mass-abuse monlist to amplify denial-of-service floods against third parties, and the reply also leaks the server's client IPs. The owner loses no control or data, so information.
salesperson_line: Attackers can use this time server to flood other websites with traffic, and it reveals which computers use it.

reason: Open resolvers are mass-abused as amplifiers in denial-of-service attacks on others, and they can reveal lookup history through cache probing. The owner loses no control or data.
salesperson_line: Attackers can use this server to blast other sites with traffic, and it can hint at which sites staff visit.

reason: The scanner already got in with the community string, so an attacker can too and pull device details, interfaces and network maps. Default community strings are mass-scanned. This shows read access only, so I chose information over partial.
salesperson_line: Anyone can pull detailed information about this network device and the network behind it using a common default password.

reason: Internet-facing RDP is a top ransomware entry point through mass password guessing and stolen credentials. Getting in requires a valid password for this target, so automatable is no. A successful login gives full control of the machine.
salesperson_line: This Windows remote login faces the internet; criminals constantly guess passwords on these, and one success gives them the whole machine.

reason: Legacy RDP encryption can be intercepted by anyone on the network path using public tools, capturing credentials and session content. That requires a network position, and I chose partial because it captures sessions, not the machine.
salesperson_line: Someone positioned between staff and this server could spy on remote sessions and steal login passwords.

reason: Internet-facing SMBv1 is still mass-scanned by EternalBlue-style worms, but full takeover requires the MS17-010 patch to be missing, which this finding doesn't confirm. Without that flaw, an attacker needs credentials and gets file access, so partial.
salesperson_line: This server uses the outdated file-sharing protocol that WannaCry ransomware spread through; if a patch is missing, it can be taken over.

reason: Botnets like Mirai mass-scan Telnet and log in with default credentials, and logins travel unencrypted. We don't know these devices use default passwords, so automatable is no. A successful login gives total control.
salesperson_line: This device accepts unencrypted remote logins from the internet; botnets constantly try default passwords on these to take them over.

reason: Anyone can read host metrics including kernel version, hostname, mounted disks and running services. That helps target later attacks but gives no control or data.
salesperson_line: Anyone can read detailed technical information about this server, helping attackers pick which weaknesses to try.

reason: Attackers routinely use search engines and crawlers to find open directory listings and download whatever they expose. I chose information over partial because the listing itself shows file names, and whether sensitive files are present varies.
salesperson_line: Anyone can browse a list of files on this web server and may find files never meant to be public.

reason: Internet-facing MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL are mass password-guessed by malware and ransomware crews. Getting in requires this server's credentials. A successful login gives total control of the data.
salesperson_line: This database is open to the internet; criminals constantly guess passwords on these, and success exposes all its data.

reason: The server accepts connections from any caller name, and public DICOM tools can then query and download patient images. I chose partial because accepting a connection doesn't prove queries and downloads are allowed, and poc because I don't know of widespread abuse.
salesperson_line: This medical imaging server accepts connections from anyone online, which can let outsiders look up and download patient scans.

reason: POODLE and DROWN let an attacker on the network path decrypt parts of traffic, such as cookies. That requires a network position and only exposes some session data.
salesperson_line: Someone positioned between users and this service could decrypt parts of their traffic, such as login sessions.

reason: No public method breaks a 1024-bit RSA key, and the evidence certificates are self-signed, so MD5 collisions don't apply. If the key were broken, an attacker on the network path could impersonate the service or read some traffic.
salesperson_line: This service's encryption is weaker than today's standard, making it easier for a well-funded attacker to eavesdrop or impersonate it.

reason: An end-of-life OS has no direct attack path of its own; it just won't get fixes for future flaws. I chose information because the finding only reveals the OS version.
salesperson_line: This system no longer receives security fixes, so any newly discovered weakness will stay open for good.

reason: A simple unauthenticated request downloads the DVR config, which includes stored credentials, and public exploit modules exist. I chose partial over total because the flaw itself only discloses the config, even though the credentials inside can lead to takeover.
salesperson_line: Anyone can download this camera recorder's settings, including logins, and use them to watch or control the cameras.

reason: An unauthenticated connection with a database name starting with a hyphen can corrupt server files. Running code requires valid credentials, so I rated the no-login path as partial.
salesperson_line: Anyone who can reach this database can corrupt its files and crash it; anyone with a login could run commands on it.

reason: Anyone can send crafted heartbeats to read up to 64 KB of memory per request, and this was exploited at mass scale. Each read is random, so it is partial even though private keys and passwords can leak.
salesperson_line: Anyone online can repeatedly pull chunks of this server's memory, which can contain passwords, session cookies or its encryption key.

reason: FREAK needs an attacker on the network path to force affected clients onto weak export encryption and then break it. That gives access to some session traffic.
salesperson_line: Someone positioned between users and a server could weaken the encryption and read some of their traffic.

reason: A single crafted Range header crashes the server or leaks memory, and this was mass-scanned and exploited. Public exploits never reliably achieved code execution, so I chose partial over total.
salesperson_line: Anyone can crash this Windows web server with one request and may be able to pull data from its memory.

reason: A malformed HTTP header makes Jetty return leftover memory in the error reply, which can include other users' requests and session tokens. The leaked chunks are random, so partial.
salesperson_line: Anyone can trick this web server into leaking pieces of other users' requests, possibly including their passwords or sessions.

reason: Logjam requires an attacker on the network path to rewrite the TLS handshake down to weak export encryption and break it. That exposes some session traffic.
salesperson_line: Someone positioned between users and this server could downgrade its encryption and read their traffic.

reason: A single crafted WebDAV PROPFIND request runs code on IIS 6, and it was exploited in the wild, including by crypto-mining campaigns. That gives total control.
salesperson_line: Anyone can take over this old Windows web server with a single specially crafted request.

reason: An unauthenticated request to /common/info.cgi returns model, firmware, network and device details but no credentials or video. That helps target later attacks.
salesperson_line: Anyone can read this camera's model, software version and network details, helping them pick an attack.

reason: BlueKeep lets an unauthenticated attacker run code over RDP before login, it is wormable, and it was exploited in the wild. That gives total control at the SYSTEM level.
salesperson_line: Anyone can take full control of this Windows machine remotely without a password; criminals have already used this flaw.

reason: A crafted URL reads any file on the VPN appliance without logging in, including stored plaintext credentials and session data. It was mass-exploited by ransomware and state actors, and arbitrary file read covers all the data the appliance holds.
salesperson_line: Anyone can pull passwords straight off this company's VPN and use them to walk into the internal network.

reason: This command injection needs admin credentials, which attackers usually got by pairing it with CVE-2019-1653, and the pair was exploited in the wild. On its own it requires credentials, so automatable is no; it gives root on the router.
salesperson_line: Anyone with the router's admin login can take complete control of it, and attackers have been stealing those logins.

reason: Unauthenticated requests download the router config and diagnostics, including credential hashes, and this was mass-scanned within days of disclosure. I chose partial because the flaw only discloses data, though the credentials can lead to takeover.
salesperson_line: Anyone can download this router's full settings, including login details, opening the door to taking it over.

reason: SMBGhost lets an unauthenticated attacker run code with crafted SMBv3 compression packets, public exploits exist, and it is listed as exploited in the wild. That gives SYSTEM-level control.
salesperson_line: Anyone who can reach this Windows file-sharing service could take full control of the machine without a password.

reason: ProxyLogon's request forgery flaw lets an unauthenticated attacker act as the Exchange server, read any mailbox, and chain to code execution. Exchange servers were mass-exploited worldwide.
salesperson_line: Anyone can read every email on this company's mail server and plant a backdoor, as happened to tens of thousands of firms.

reason: This deserialization bug runs code as SYSTEM but needs admin rights or a chain with CVE-2021-26855; it was exploited in the ProxyLogon campaigns. Alone it requires access the attacker doesn't have, so automatable is no.
salesperson_line: An attacker with any foothold on this mail server can take complete control of it; this was used in mass attacks.

reason: This flaw writes arbitrary files, enabling web shells, but needs authentication or a chain with CVE-2021-26855; it was used in the ProxyLogon campaigns. Alone it requires access, so automatable is no.
salesperson_line: An attacker who gets a foothold on this mail server can plant a hidden backdoor and fully control it.

reason: This flaw writes arbitrary files, the web-shell step of ProxyLogon, but needs authentication or a chain with CVE-2021-26855. It was mass-exploited as part of that chain.
salesperson_line: An attacker who gets a foothold on this mail server can plant a hidden backdoor and fully control it.

reason: The description only says 'Exchange RCE', with no attack path, authentication requirement or network position. I can't reliably recall its prerequisites or exploitation status, so I am not rating it rather than guessing.
salesperson_line: This mail server may have a serious remote takeover flaw; details are needed to judge how urgent it is.

reason: This ProxyShell step abuses mailbox export to write a web shell, but it needs Exchange admin access, normally obtained via CVE-2021-34473 and CVE-2021-34523. The chain was mass-exploited by ransomware groups.
salesperson_line: An attacker who gets into this mail server's admin tools can plant a backdoor and fully control it.

reason: ProxyShell's path confusion lets unauthenticated requests reach Exchange backend services. Combined with CVE-2021-34523 (fixed in the same April 2021 update, so present on the same unpatched servers), it leads to full takeover and was mass-exploited.
salesperson_line: Anyone can break into this company's mail server without a password; ransomware gangs mass-exploited this exact flaw.

reason: This ProxyShell flaw raises access to Exchange admin PowerShell but requires backend access, normally gained via CVE-2021-34473. Alone it isn't reachable from the internet, so automatable is no.
salesperson_line: An attacker who gets a foothold on this mail server can give themselves full admin control; this was used in mass attacks.

reason: A path-traversal URL under /public/plugins/ reads local files without logging in, such as the Grafana database and config with data-source credentials, and it was exploited in the wild. It is limited to files the Grafana process can read, so partial.
salesperson_line: Anyone can download files from this dashboard server, including stored passwords to the company's other databases.

reason: A buffer overflow in the login page's username and password fields gives unauthenticated code execution on the router. I know of no credible reports of mass exploitation, so I chose poc.
salesperson_line: Anyone can take full control of this router through its login page without knowing the password.

reason: The attacker needs a streaming connection, meaning a valid API key or a child agent's machine ID, to inject commands through an alert. Commands run as the low-privilege netdata user, so partial.
salesperson_line: An attacker who can send data to this monitoring server can make it run their commands.

reason: A child agent's machine ID, visible to anyone who can reach that child, works as the parent's streaming API key, letting an attacker push forged data. It requires a separately exposed child and is limited to the monitoring stream.
salesperson_line: An outsider could feed fake data into this monitoring system and, combined with another flaw, run commands on it.

reason: Unauthenticated command injection through downloader.php gives a shell on the solar monitoring device. Mirai-style botnets actively exploit it.
salesperson_line: Anyone can take over this solar monitoring device; botnets are already hijacking these.

reason: Spoofed proxy headers make remote requests look local, allowing passwordless admin login where local logins skip passwords. Mass compromise of Emby servers followed in 2023, and admin access leads to code execution through plugins.
salesperson_line: Anyone can log in to this media server as admin with no password and take it over; this happened to many servers in 2023.

reason: The unauthenticated config-update function on exposed RocketMQ components runs arbitrary commands. Botnets such as DreamBus exploit it in the wild.
salesperson_line: Anyone can run commands on this messaging server without a password; botnets are actively doing this.

reason: Only an existing administrator can point the encoder path at a network share and run an executable. It needs admin credentials but gives code execution on the server.
salesperson_line: Anyone who gets this media server's admin login can run any program on the machine.

reason: The '@file' expansion in Jenkins CLI arguments leaks files without logging in, and it has been used in ransomware intrusions. Unauthenticated attackers only see the first lines of each file, so I chose partial over total.
salesperson_line: Anyone can read parts of files on this build server, including secret keys that can lead to a full takeover.

reason: CitrixBleed 2 lets unauthenticated requests leak gateway memory, including session tokens that allow session hijacking. It was exploited in the wild soon after disclosure. Each request leaks only some memory, so partial.
salesperson_line: Anyone can steal logged-in sessions from this company's remote-access gateway and get inside without a password.

reason: This is the same HTTP.sys flaw as CVE-2015-1635: one crafted Range header crashes the server or leaks memory, and it was mass-scanned. Public exploits never reliably achieved code execution, so partial.
salesperson_line: Anyone can crash this Windows web server with one request and may be able to pull data from its memory.

reason: EternalBlue gives unauthenticated SYSTEM-level code execution over SMBv1. It powered the WannaCry and NotPetya worms and is still mass-exploited.
salesperson_line: Anyone can take full control of this Windows machine remotely; this is the flaw WannaCry ransomware used.
